title: Total Hardness Calculation (meq/L & mg/L as CaCO3)
description:
A groundwater supply sample contains 60.0 mg/L of Ca2+ and 24.0 mg/L of Mg2+. The equivalent weights are: Ca2+ = 20.04 mg/meq, Mg2+ = 12.15 mg/meq, and CaCO3 = 50.04 mg/meq.

1. Convert the calcium and magnesium concentrations into milliequivalents per liter (meq/L).
2. Calculate the Total Hardness (TH) expressed in mg/L as CaCO3.
3. Classify the degree of water hardness (Soft, Moderately Hard, Hard, or Very Hard).

options.label: A
options.text: Ca = 2.99 meq/L; Mg = 1.98 meq/L; Total Hardness = 249 mg/L as CaCO3 (Very Hard Water > 180 mg/L)
options.feedback: Correct! meq/L = (mg/L) / Equivalent Weight. For Ca2+: 60.0 / 20.04 = 2.994 meq/L. For Mg2+: 24.0 / 12.15 = 1.975 meq/L. Total hardness meq/L = 2.994 + 1.975 = 4.969 meq/L. Total Hardness as CaCO3 = 4.969 meq/L × 50.04 mg/meq = 248.7 mg/L as CaCO3 (most nearly 249 mg/L). Waters with TH > 180 mg/L as CaCO3 are classified as 'Very Hard'.

options.label: B
options.text: Ca = 1.50 meq/L; Mg = 0.99 meq/L; Total Hardness = 125 mg/L as CaCO3 (Moderately Hard Water)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Divided by atomic weight instead of equivalent weight (EW = MW / 2 for divalent ions Ca2+ and Mg2+).

options.label: C
options.text: Ca = 3.00 meq/L; Mg = 2.00 meq/L; Total Hardness = 84.0 mg/L as CaCO3 (Direct addition of mg/L: 60 + 24)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Added raw mg/L directly (60 + 24 = 84 mg/L) without converting to calcium carbonate equivalents (mg/L as CaCO3).

options.label: D
options.text: Ca = 6.00 meq/L; Mg = 4.00 meq/L; Total Hardness = 500 mg/L as CaCO3 (Doubled valence)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiplied valence by 2 instead of dividing molecular weight by valence.

hint: Convert each ion concentration to meq/L using meq/L = (mg/L) / EW, then multiply the sum of divalent cations (Ca2+ + Mg2+) by 50.04 mg/meq (the equivalent weight of CaCO3).
shortcut: Quick NCEES multiplier rule: Ca2+ (mg/L) × 2.50 ≈ Ca Hardness as CaCO3 (60 × 2.50 = 150). Mg2+ (mg/L) × 4.12 ≈ Mg Hardness as CaCO3 (24 × 4.12 = 98.9). Total = 150 + 98.9 = 248.9 ≈ 249 mg/L as CaCO3!
fifthGrader: Think of dissolved calcium and magnesium like tiny invisible sticky rock magnets floating in water. A calcium rock weighs different than a magnesium rock, so we use a magic 'carbonate ruler' to convert both into matching units. Then we add them up! Anything over 180 is very hard water that steals your soap bubbles and leaves ring-around-the-bathtub!

title: Carbonate vs Noncarbonate Hardness (Alkalinity Partition)
description:
A comprehensive municipal water quality report reveals a Total Hardness (TH) of 250 mg/L as CaCO3 and a Total Alkalinity (Alk) of 180 mg/L as CaCO3 (primarily bicarbonate, HCO3-).

1. Determine the Carbonate Hardness (CH) in mg/L as CaCO3.
2. Determine the Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH) in mg/L as CaCO3.
3. Identify which chemical treatment (boiling/lime vs soda ash) is required to remove each hardness fraction.

options.label: A
options.text: Carbonate Hardness = 180 mg/L as CaCO3; Noncarbonate Hardness = 70 mg/L as CaCO3 (CH removed by Lime; NCH removed by Soda Ash)
options.feedback: Correct! When Total Hardness > Alkalinity: Carbonate Hardness (CH) = Alkalinity = 180 mg/L as CaCO3 (associated with HCO3- and CO3 2- anions). Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH) = Total Hardness - Alkalinity = 250 - 180 = 70 mg/L as CaCO3 (associated with SO4 2- and Cl- anions). Carbonate hardness can be precipitated with hydrated lime Ca(OH)2 or heat, whereas noncarbonate hardness requires soda ash Na2CO3.

options.label: B
options.text: Carbonate Hardness = 250 mg/L as CaCO3; Noncarbonate Hardness = 0 mg/L as CaCO3 (All hardness is carbonate)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Carbonate hardness cannot exceed total alkalinity. Since Alkalinity is 180 mg/L, the maximum carbonate hardness is 180 mg/L.

options.label: C
options.text: Carbonate Hardness = 70 mg/L as CaCO3; Noncarbonate Hardness = 180 mg/L as CaCO3 (Swapped roles)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Swapped carbonate and noncarbonate fractions. Carbonate hardness is capped by alkalinity.

options.label: D
options.text: Carbonate Hardness = 125 mg/L as CaCO3; Noncarbonate Hardness = 125 mg/L as CaCO3 (50/50 split)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Hardness does not partition evenly; it must be calculated using the NCEES rule: CH = min(TH, Alkalinity).

hint: NCEES Reference Handbook Rule: If Alkalinity < Total Hardness, then Carbonate Hardness = Alkalinity, and Noncarbonate Hardness = Total Hardness - Alkalinity. If Alkalinity ≥ Total Hardness, then Carbonate Hardness = Total Hardness, and Noncarbonate Hardness = 0.
shortcut: Look at the water bar chart: Alkalinity is the green bar (180). Because 180 is less than Total Hardness (250), the green bar lines up with Carbonate Hardness (180). Any hardness sticking out past the green bar is Noncarbonate Hardness: 250 - 180 = 70 mg/L as CaCO3!
fifthGrader: Think of Carbonate Hardness like 'Temporary Hardness' that is holding hands with bicarbonate shields. If you boil tea in a kettle, they fall out as crunchy flakes on the kettle bottom. But Noncarbonate Hardness is 'Permanent Hardness' holding hands with stubborn sulfate buddies. Boiling does nothing to them — you need magic softening soda powder (soda ash) to kick them out!

title: Lime Dosage for Carbonate Hardness & Free CO2
description:
A municipal water softening plant treats groundwater with the following chemical characteristics:
• Free Carbon Dioxide (CO2) = 15.0 mg/L as CaCO3
• Calcium (Ca2+) = 140.0 mg/L as CaCO3
• Magnesium (Mg2+) = 60.0 mg/L as CaCO3
• Total Alkalinity = 150.0 mg/L as CaCO3

Calculate the stoichiometric hydrated lime Ca(OH)2 dosage in mg/L as CaCO3 required to neutralize the dissolved CO2 and precipitate all calcium carbonate hardness.

options.label: A
options.text: Lime Dose = 165 mg/L as CaCO3 (CO2 neutralization + Ca-Alkalinity precipitation)
options.feedback: Correct! Lime first neutralizes free CO2: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O (15 mg/L as CaCO3). Lime then reacts with ALL bicarbonate alkalinity (OH- + HCO3- → CO3 2- + H2O), regardless of which cation it is paired with: 150 mg/L as CaCO3. Of that, 140 mg/L precipitates as CaCO3 with the calcium. Stoichiometric lime dose (no Mg removal, no excess) = CO2 + Alkalinity = 15 + 150 = 165 mg/L as CaCO3.

options.label: B
options.text: Lime Dose = 150 mg/L as CaCO3 (Ignored dissolved CO2 gas)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Forgotten to add lime for free CO2. Free CO2 consumes lime before any hardness can precipitate.

options.label: C
options.text: Lime Dose = 215 mg/L as CaCO3 (Added total calcium + CO2 + magnesium)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Overestimated by adding all calcium plus magnesium without distinguishing between carbonate and noncarbonate hardness.

options.label: D
options.text: Lime Dose = 15 mg/L as CaCO3 (Only neutralized CO2)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only provided lime to react with dissolved CO2, failing to add lime to precipitate calcium bicarbonate hardness.

hint: Remember that dissolved CO2 gas in water reacts immediately with lime: CO2 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O. You must satisfy the CO2 demand first, then add 1 equivalent of lime for each equivalent of bicarbonate alkalinity.
shortcut: Stoichiometric Lime Rule: Lime (mg/L as CaCO3) = [CO2] + [HCO3-]. 15 + 150 = 165 mg/L as CaCO3. Simple addition when all quantities are already expressed as CaCO3!
fifthGrader: Lime is like a chemical sponge. Before you can clean up the dissolved minerals, the water has fizzy carbon dioxide gas bubbles that eat your lime sponge! So you must give 15 scoops of sponge to eat the gas first, and then 150 scoops to grab the calcium carbonate. 15 + 150 = 165 scoops!

title: Soda Ash Dosage for Noncarbonate Hardness
description:
A surface water supply has a Total Hardness (TH) of 300.0 mg/L as CaCO3 and a Total Alkalinity of 200.0 mg/L as CaCO3. The raw water is treated using the lime-soda ash softening process.

Assuming all Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH) is to be completely precipitated as CaCO3 and Mg(OH)2, calculate the required stoichiometric Soda Ash (Na2CO3) dosage in mg/L as CaCO3.

options.label: A
options.text: Soda Ash Dose = 100 mg/L as CaCO3 (NCH = TH - Alkalinity = 300 - 200)
options.feedback: Correct! Soda ash (Na2CO3) is added strictly to remove Noncarbonate Hardness (hardness associated with sulfate SO4 2- and chloride Cl-). The reaction is: CaSO4 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3↓ + Na2SO4. Each equivalent of NCH requires exactly 1 equivalent of soda ash. Here: NCH = TH - Alkalinity = 300 - 200 = 100 mg/L as CaCO3. Therefore, required soda ash dose is 100 mg/L as CaCO3.

options.label: B
options.text: Soda Ash Dose = 300 mg/L as CaCO3 (Dosed for Total Hardness)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Soda ash is NOT dosed for total hardness; carbonate hardness is precipitated by lime. Soda ash only treats noncarbonate hardness.

options.label: C
options.text: Soda Ash Dose = 200 mg/L as CaCO3 (Dosed for Alkalinity)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Dosed soda ash for alkalinity instead of noncarbonate hardness.

options.label: D
options.text: Soda Ash Dose = 50 mg/L as CaCO3 (Assumed 50% recovery)
options.feedback: Incorrect. Arbitrarily halved the stoichiometric dosage.

hint: Soda ash provides carbonate ions (CO3 2-) to pair with calcium associated with strong acid anions (SO4 2-, Cl-). Stoichiometric soda ash dose = Noncarbonate Hardness = Total Hardness - Alkalinity.
shortcut: Soda Ash Dose (as CaCO3) = Total Hardness - Alkalinity = 300 - 200 = 100 mg/L as CaCO3. Always 1:1 on an equivalent basis!
fifthGrader: Soda ash is a magic white powder that only cares about the stubborn noncarbonate rocks. We see 300 total rocks minus 200 temporary rocks = 100 stubborn rocks. So we need exactly 100 scoops of soda ash powder!

title: Excess Lime Softening (Magnesium Removal)
description: To precipitate Magnesium during softening, the pH must be raised to around 11.0. This requires an 'excess lime' dose. If the total Mg2+ is 80 mg/L as CaCO3, and the standard excess lime dose is 35 mg/L as CaCO3, the total lime required for Mg removal (excluding CO2 and HCO3) is:
hint: Lime required for Mg removal = Mg2+ concentration + Excess Lime.
shortcut: Magnesium is stubborn! It requires 1 part lime to react with the alkalinity, 1 part lime to precipitate the Mg, PLUS an extra 35 mg/L to drive the pH to 11.
fifthGrader: Magnesium rocks only melt when the water is super basic (pH 11). We have to add extra 'excess' lime just to push the pH up high enough!

title: Ion Exchange Softening Capacity
description: An ion exchange softener has a resin capacity of 20 kilograins per cubic foot (kgr/ft3). The resin volume is 50 ft3. The raw water has a hardness of 300 mg/L as CaCO3. What is the maximum volume of water (gallons) that can be softened before regeneration?
hint: 1 grain per gallon (gpg) = 17.1 mg/L. Total Capacity (grains) = Volume * Capacity. Gallons = Total Capacity / Hardness (in gpg).
shortcut: Convert 300 mg/L to grains per gallon: 300 / 17.1 = 17.5 gpg. Total grains = 20,000 * 50 = 1,000,000. 1,000,000 / 17.5 = 57,142 gallons.
fifthGrader: Think of the resin like a sponge that can hold exactly 1,000,000 pieces of dirt. If every gallon of water has 17.5 pieces of dirt, how many gallons until the sponge is full?

title: Softened Water Blending (Bypass)
description: A treatment plant must deliver water with a hardness of 100 mg/L. The raw water has a hardness of 350 mg/L, and the ion exchange softener reduces hardness to 10 mg/L. What percentage of the flow should bypass the softener?
hint: Use the mass balance equation: Q_total * C_target = Q_bypass * C_raw + Q_soft * C_soft. Let Q_total = 1.
fifthGrader: If you mix super salty water with pure water, you get medium salty water. We are just using math to figure out the perfect recipe for the mix!

title: Equivalent Weight Conversion
description: A water sample has 96 mg/L of Sulfate (SO4 2-). The atomic weights are S=32.1, O=16.0. The equivalent weight of CaCO3 is 50.0 g/eq. What is the Sulfate concentration in mg/L as CaCO3?
hint: Molecular weight of SO4 = 32.1 + 4(16) = 96.1 g/mol. Charge is 2, so Equivalent Weight = 96.1 / 2 = 48.05 g/eq. Multiply mg/L by (50 / 48.05).
shortcut: The equivalent weight of Sulfate is roughly 48. Since 96 / 48 = 2 meq/L. Multiply by 50 to get 100 mg/L as CaCO3.
fifthGrader: Scientists like to measure everything using the exact same ruler (CaCO3). We are just converting Sulfate's weight into the universal ruler's weight!

title: Alkalinity Relationships
description: A water sample has a pH of 10.2. The Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P) is 40 mg/L as CaCO3 and the Total alkalinity (T) is 120 mg/L as CaCO3. The concentration of Carbonate (CO3 2-) alkalinity is most nearly:
hint: Check the Alkalinity Relationship Table. If P < 1/2 T, then Carbonate = 2*P and Bicarbonate = T - 2P.
shortcut: P = 40, T = 120. Since 40 is less than half of 120, Carbonate is 2 * P = 80 mg/L as CaCO3.
fifthGrader: Alkalinity comes in three flavors: Hydroxide, Carbonate, and Bicarbonate. Depending on the pH, we can figure out exactly how much of each flavor is in the water!

title: Split Treatment Softening
description: In a split treatment softening process, a portion of the raw water bypasses the first stage (excess lime) and is mixed with the first stage effluent in the second stage. The primary purpose of this bypassed flow is to:
hint: The first stage operates at pH 11 to drop out Mg. The bypassed raw water contains HCO3- and CO2, which naturally lowers the pH and provides carbonate to react with excess Ca.
shortcut: Bypassing raw water saves money! You don't need as much CO2 for recarbonation because the raw water naturally neutralizes the high pH of the first stage.
fifthGrader: Instead of adding expensive acid to fix the super basic water from the first tank, we just mix in some normal raw water. It naturally cools off the chemicals and saves money!
